The bank’s statute vested the decision over transfers in the Secretary, 
and Duane interpreted the Act as authorizing the removal of deposits only 
if the Secretary determined, in his independent judgment, that deposits 
were unsafe in the national bank. Jackson successfully secured from his 
attorney general, Roger Taney, an opinion endorsing presidential authority 
to direct the removal, but Duane continued to resist. Jackson then 
summarily removed Duane and placed the Treasury Department 
temporarily under the control of Taney, who commenced the withdrawals. 
The removal controversy ultimately ehcited House resolutions supporting 
the president, but also a still-unique Senate resolution censuring the 
president and challenging his removal power. Nonetheless, near the end of 
his second term, Jackson’s Senate alhes successfully managed a vote that 
expunged the censure, effectively vindicating his position. HAROLD H.

Tenure in Office Act. The Union victory at Appomattox on April 9, 
1865, and the assassination of Abraham Lincoln less than a week later 
intensified what was already poised to become a serious confrontation 
between the elected branches over Reconstruction. The Republican- 
dominated Congress was determined not to recognize the governments of 
secessionist states except under conditions more strict than even T Jncoin 
had recommended. But Andrew Johnson—a former enslaver who had 
supported emancipation only to preserve the Union—sought a version of 
reconstruction only partial and far more permissive. As Johnson’s term 
progressed, tensions increased between the President and members of his 
inherited cabinet, who sought to undermine bis policies. Most notable 
among them was Edwin Stanton, Lincoln’s Secretary of War.
Congress responded by enacting the Tenure in Office Act of 1867 over 
Johnsons veto. The Act provided that any civil officer appointed with the 
Senate s advice and consent would serve until a successor would be 
appointed by the President, also with the Senate’s advice and consent. It 
went on to specify that the Secretaries of State, of the Treasury, of War, of 
the Navy, and of the Interior, as well as the Postmaster General and the 
Attorney General would hold their respective offices “for and during the 
term of the President by whom they may have been appointed, and for one 
month thereafter, subject to removal by and with the advice and consent of 
the Senate.” Lest there be any doubt as to Congress’s intention to 
hamstring Johnson specifically, its final paragraph provided that “every 
person who shall violate any of the provisions of this section shall be 
deemed guilty of a high misdemeanor.” Act of March 2, 1867, 14 Stat.428, 
432.
